text.p: By Peter Campbell*
BAREFOOT BUSINESS EXECUTIVES ABOARD CAMBRIA
DENIS O'NEIL has made his magnificent yacht Cambria available for VIP guests to participate in -- and make their $250-a-head contributions to -- Sunday's Sail for Cancer.
But there are a couple of stipulations -- no food or drink on board the restored timber vessel, and definitely no shoes.

So we will see some of Sydney's corporate leaders and their partners barefooted on the teak-laid decks of Cambria after a pleasant (shoes and jackets, of course) buffet luncheon at the Royal Sydney Yacht Squadron (RSYS).

Up to 40 people can be accommodated on board Cambria for the Sail for Cancer, which raises much-needed funds for the Leo & Jenny Leukaemia and Cancer Foundation. While there are still a few vacancies, the response has been exceptional.
Cambria will follow the Sail for Cancer fun race and be on hand for the relaunch of the windjammer James Craig after its painstaking restoration by the Sydney Maritime Museum.

Among those who will enjoy the barefoot day aboard Cambria will be Ord Minnet chief executive CHRIS GORMAN, who incidentally notched up third on handicap in last week's Wollongong-to-Sydney ocean race with his J-44 sloop, Adria. His guest on board will be JOHN FIRTH-SMITH.

Former Olympic sailor MARK BETHWAITE, now chief executive of RGC, will forsake Laser sailing to be joined by his wife CAROLINE and friends. Also aboard will be Mr and Mrs LYN R. ANDERSON, he being chief of Russell Reynolds & Associates Inc, along with ROD and ANNIE COOK from Data Centre. Strong support has also come from Westpac Banking Corporation, with eight or 10 senior executives and partners expected to join the crew.

NIGEL STOKE, head of the syndicate of RSYS members who own the former Sydney-to-Hobart line honours winner Fidelis, will be overseas but will be represented by his wife, SHEENAGH, while others aboard will include TONY and LUCY SUNMAN of Woollahra Solutions.
If you are interested, a phone call to JANE at the Leo & Jenny Foundation could secure a last-minute berth aboard Cambria. The number is 9371 0400.

So far some 175 yachts have signed up and the massive regatta gets under way at 11 a.m. Sunday. The fleet will sail a course down to Lady Jane, back around Shark and Clarke Islands for a massive raft-up in Athol Bight.
BT GLOBAL BOOM FOR ENTERTAINMENT BUSINESS

The arrival, almost en masse last Sunday evening, of the fleet of one-design, steel 60-footers in the BT Global Challenge's sprint leg across the Tasman, resulted in some high-flying functions by the sponsors of individual yachts.

Courtaulds, which has a yacht in the race and presented the prize for the Wellington-Sydney leg, has invited about 150 people to the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia next Tuesday, while the British Consul-General held a prestigious black tie dinner for organisers and skippers at the Royal Sydney Golf Club last Tuesday.

Other sponsors are holding functions during the two weeks the 14 yachts are in Sydney and yesterday they got on to the football bandwagon with the Sydney Swans going for a sail aboard two of the competing yachts.

Winner of the leg was Save the Children, which came from 11th in fleet to cross the line more than an hour ahead of Ocean 4, the yacht which had taken line honours in the two previous legs from Southampton to Rio de Janeiro and from there to Wellington, New Zealand, rounding Cape Horn.

Among the crew of Save the Children was young Sydney sailor ROD STEVENS, while occasionally controversial newspaper columnist PIERS AKERMANN was the only Australian journalist to take up the offer of joining a yacht for the Tasman Sea sprint.
However, three English yachting writers were aboard other yachts and Perth-based JOHN ROBERSON will sail the tough leg from Sydney to Cape Town, starting Sunday, March 2.
PORT LINCOLN RACE TO FUTURE SHOCK

Melbourne yachtsman PETER HANSEN completed a rare double last weekend when he sailed his Melbourne-to-Hobart record-breaker PL Lease Future Shock to a line honours victory in the 47th Adelaide-to-Port Lincoln race.

While Future Shock's time for the 172-nautical mile race was outside the record, a big fleet of 101 yachts -- five more than the 1996 Telstra Sydney-to-Hobart fleet -- set sail from Outer Harbour last Friday, including a strong contingent of racing and cruising yachts from Melbourne.
All 101 boats completed the course in the easy sailing conditions across the Gulf of St Vincent and Spencers Gulf, many then competing in this week's Lincoln Week regatta.

Future Shock, the much travelled Elliott-55, sailed the course in 21 hours and three minutes to end a run of line honours victories by Helsal II, the famous pocket maxi owned by veteran Adelaide yachtsman KEITH FLINT.
Local Port Adelaide boat Scavenger, skippered by PETER BARWICK finished a close third, with first place on corrected time going to Metereo, skippered by MARK HANEN.
STRONG INTEREST IN MOOLOOLABA RACE

Entries close next Friday for Middle Harbour Yacht Club's 34th annual Sydney-to-Mooloolaba race, the popular end-of-season 489-miler up the New South Wales coast to Queensland's Sunshine Coast north of Brisbane.

The race, starting on Saturday, March 22, is the final race of the Blue Water Pointscore and the fleet will certainly include most of those yachts in the running for a top place overall in the prestigious trophy.

Among the International Measurement System racing yachts expected to compete will be SYD FISCHER's Ragamuffin, RAY ROBERTS's BZW Challenge, ROGER HICKMAN's Atara, MARTIN JAMES's pocket maxi Infinity and DICK VOORDEHAKE's Rapscallion, which scored a win and a second place in last weekend's Cruising Yacht Club races to and from Wollongong.

Among the 30-plus entries already received is PETER WALKER's evergreen maxi Foxtel Amazon, looking for its fourth line honours win. Club officials are also hoping to see WARWICK MILLER enter his 66-footer Exile, which last weekend broke the race record for the 45-nautical mile overnight dash from Sydney to Wollongong.
WET WOMEN ON WATER
Spare a thought for the 70 intrepid women sailors who braved last week's appalling weather to contest the Women on Water Nortel Asia Pacific Women's Regatta on Sydney Harbour.

Royal Sydney Yacht Squadron had to abandon racing on the Wednesday because of fog and rain but in the end the two days of coaching and the scheduled nine races were completed, with the women sailing J-24s in the open division and Elliott-5.9s in the youth division.

The open division was decided in the final race between 1988 Olympic partners NICOLA BETHWAITE, skippering Convicts' Revenge, and KARYN GOJNICH, helming Computer Results Team, with BETHWAITE taking out the title.
In the under-25 youth division, the team from the Royal Prince Alfred Yacht Club of KATIE SPITHILL, KATE DOWNING and SONJA KNAPMAN won five of the nine races.
PETER GILMOUR JOINS JAPANESE CUP TEAM

PETER GILMOUR, Australia's best match racing helmsman and former America's Cup skipper, has left our shores to become a resident of Japan and thus qualify over the next three years to skipper the Japanese challenger for the America's Cup in 2000.
GILMOUR, now number two in world match racing rankings, was head coach in Japan's 1995 America's Cup attempt, but he was prohibited from competing due to nationality limits.

The 37-year-old former Perth sailor, his wife CHRISTINE and their three young boys will be based in Yokahama, near Tokyo, as he takes up his full-time role as sailing director and skipper for the Japanese challenger.

GILMOUR has been sailing with Japanese members of his America's Cup 2000 crew for the past three years on the international match racing and offshore racing circuits. They finished third in last week's Australia Cup back in his home waters on Perth's Swan River.
Their next international contests will be sailing the ILC-46 Swing in next week's SORC regatta in Miami and the ACI Cup in Rovinj, Croatia, in April.
The Japanese Challenge for the America's Cup has again received strong corporate support, with the syndicate membership including senior representatives of major Japanese economic organisations.

Meanwhile, GILMOUR's former America's Cup partner (and still business partner), yacht designer IAIN MURRAY, is remaining tight-lipped about my report last week that he and DENNIS O'NEIL are planning an Australian challenge against the Royal New Zealand Yacht Squadron.

However, I can report that MURRAY is buying, at a bargain price, the remnants of the luckless oneAustralia Challenge of 1995, including the one surviving yacht, loads of sails, spare masts and other equipment, along with vital computer programmes and records.
AUSTRALIAN SUCCESS AT SAIL AUCKLAND

Australian Yachtsman of the Year and Olympic silver medallist MITCH BOOTH, with champion Laser sailor ADAM BEASHEL as a newcomer to crewing on a catamaran, scored an impressive victory last weekend in the Tornado class at Sail Auckland.
Atlanta 470 class skipper TOM KING from Melbourne, with MARK TURNBULL as crew, finished second in that class, while young Sydney world champion HEIDI GORDON won the Laser Radials.

Hong Kong's first and only Olympic gold medallist, LEE LAI-SHAN, who is now studying at Canberra's ANU, followed up her Sail Melbourne success by taking out the Mistral sailboards with Australia's NATASHA STURGES placing third.
